title: Who Gets to Define the Rules for AI? | Cohere
gist: Cohere CEO Aidan Gomez attacks Anthropic's newly published roadmap asking governments for antitrust exemptions so a handful of frontier labs can jointly set AI safety standards and pace, framing it as a cartel play analogous to the 1975 US bond-rating NRSRO system and the 1985 EU auto Block Exemption. He counters with a four-pillar alternative (internationally-developed evidence-based risk framework, mandatory transparency, evidence-scoped tiered testing, independent assurance) and pitches Cohere's sovereign, on-prem, multi-vendor enterprise AI model as the safer market structure.

themes.theme: The Cartel Framing of AI Safety Rules

insights.claim: Aidan Gomez argues the real dispute in AI regulation is not whether guardrails are needed but who writes them, who gets to participate, and whose interests the rules end up protecting.
insights.speaker: Aidan Gomez
insights.so_what: Frames the entire AI policy fight as a governance/participation contest rather than a safety-vs-no-safety debate, which is the lens to use when reading any lab-authored regulatory proposal.
insights.quote: AI needs guardrails. That is not the dispute and never has been. The dispute is over who writes them, who gets to participate and whose interests the rules are protecting.
insights.locator: AI needs guardrails paragraph

insights.claim: Gomez characterizes a small group of Silicon Valley AI labs as effectively requesting an antitrust waiver so they can jointly dictate safety rules and the pace of AI progress for the entire industry, calling this a cartel dressed as a safety measure.
insights.speaker: Aidan Gomez
insights.so_what: If regulators grant this kind of waiver, incumbent frontier labs gain a durable, government-sanctioned moat over competitors — a structural risk for smaller AI companies and investors backing them.
insights.quote: these oligopolies are now requesting to bend competition rules and be permitted to dictate the terms for everyone else. A wolf in sheep’s clothing, a cartel by any other name.
insights.locator: opening paragraph, market-dominant AI companies

insights.claim: A safety regime designed by only a few labs will rigorously test only the risk categories those labs already have systems built to assess, staying silent on everything else, which further entrenches their market position.
insights.speaker: Aidan Gomez
insights.so_what: Watch for compute-threshold-based safety regimes becoming a de facto competitive moat rather than a genuine risk-reduction tool.
insights.quote: A safety regime designed by a few labs will only be rigorous about the risks they have already built their safety systems to assess and completely quiet about everything else, further entrenching their market position and limiting competition.
insights.locator: risk in these existing frameworks paragraph

insights.claim: Gomez points to genuine scientific disagreement over how much offensive AI capability comes from raw model scale versus the orchestration/tooling 'harness' around a model, noting smaller well-orchestrated models can match large ones and that a multi-agent 'cyber swarm' is a different risk surface than a single model.
insights.speaker: Aidan Gomez
insights.so_what: Regulation built purely on compute thresholds may miss the actual risk vector (orchestrated smaller-model swarms), a gap that could matter for how agentic-AI risk gets priced and regulated.
insights.quote: A cyber swarm is a completely different risk surface than a single model. None of that shows up in a regime built exclusively around massive compute thresholds.
insights.locator: types of risk deemed relevant paragraph

insights.claim: Gomez states that AI-enabled cyber offense capability is becoming cheaper faster than cyber defenses are improving, a gap he says should worry the public as much as it worries AI builders.
insights.speaker: Aidan Gomez
insights.so_what: A widening offense/defense asymmetry from AI is a systemic risk for banks, telecoms and infrastructure operators — relevant to cybersecurity spend and insurance pricing.
insights.quote: cyber offense is getting cheaper faster than defenses are getting better. That gap should worry you as much as it worries us.
insights.locator: I run a company that builds AI systems paragraph

insights.claim: In 1975 the SEC designated three firms as Nationally Recognized Statistical Rating Organizations without publishing criteria for how others could qualify; twenty-five years later there were still only three, and those same firms went on to rate subprime mortgage securities triple-A ahead of the financial crisis.
insights.speaker: Aidan Gomez
insights.so_what: Historical case that a government-blessed, closed evaluator system can calcify into an oligopoly and fail catastrophically — the direct analogy Gomez draws to a small-lab AI safety-evaluator system.
insights.quote: Twenty five years later there were still only three of these evaluators. Then they rated subprime mortgage securities triple-A and nearly took the global economy down with them.
insights.locator: We've been here before, 1975 SEC paragraph

insights.claim: Europe's 1985 Motor Vehicle Block Exemption let car manufacturers set safety-based standards for who could sell and service vehicles, but instead of safer cars it entrenched incumbents, and it took the European Commission roughly twenty-five years of reforms to unwind.
insights.speaker: Aidan Gomez
insights.so_what: A second precedent showing safety-justified incumbent-controlled standards can take decades to reverse once regulators grant them — a caution for how long an AI antitrust waiver could persist if approved.
insights.quote: it is possible you can hold strict safety standards without handing the incumbents a monopoly on meeting them
insights.locator: Europe ran the experiment again in 1985

insights.claim: In both the 1975 bond-rating and 1985 EU auto cases, the stated goal was safety, nobody set out to build a cartel, yet the outcome was a market structure that protected incumbents and limited competition under a public-interest justification.
insights.speaker: Aidan Gomez
insights.so_what: Gomez's core analytical lesson: good intentions plus safety framing do not prevent regulatory capture — a heuristic for evaluating any new industry-authored safety-regulation proposal.
insights.quote: Nobody set out to build a cartel in either case. In both cases, the stated goal was safety. But the result was a market structure that protected incumbents and limited competition
insights.locator: Nobody set out to build a cartel paragraph

themes.theme: What Anthropic's Roadmap Actually Asks For

insights.claim: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei published a roadmap asking governments for antitrust exemptions so that a handful of the most powerful AI labs, based in one country, could jointly agree on shared safety standards and limits to how fast the technology advances — coordination that would otherwise be illegal collusion between competitors.
insights.speaker: Aidan Gomez
insights.so_what: A concrete policy proposal to track: if an antitrust waiver for coordinated AI safety standards gains legislative traction, it would materially reshape competitive dynamics across the entire AI sector.
insights.quote: the plan asks governments for a narrow antitrust waiver to make that coordination lawful
insights.locator: What's Being Proposed section

insights.claim: Under the proposal as Gomez describes it, every other AI developer would be required to follow whatever standards the small group of participating labs settles on, with no opportunity for those excluded developers or wider society to weigh in.
insights.speaker: Aidan Gomez
insights.so_what: A binding-on-non-participants structure would functionally let a handful of companies set compliance costs for the entire industry, a major competitive and regulatory risk for smaller AI firms.
insights.quote: it also asks governments to require every other AI developer to blindly follow whatever the participants settle on
insights.locator: This is not a question of adding paragraph

insights.claim: The proposal's implied entry requirements for legitimate safety compliance — vast computing power, continuous monitoring infrastructure, dedicated security organizations, resident evaluator teams, shutdown architecture, and deep government relationships — are things only the largest labs can currently meet.
insights.speaker: Aidan Gomez
insights.so_what: These requirements could function as a de facto barrier to entry, disadvantaging smaller labs and startups seeking to be recognized as compliant — relevant to competitive positioning in AI investing.
insights.quote: Vast computing power. Continuous monitoring infrastructure. Dedicated security organizations. Resident evaluator teams with desks and badges. Shutdown architecture.
insights.locator: The entry requirements set out in the proposal

insights.claim: Gomez says the pool of 'independent' evaluators referenced in the proposal is already small and funded by the same handful of organizations that the frontier labs proposing the framework repeatedly rely on, implying a built-in conflict of interest.
insights.speaker: Aidan Gomez
insights.so_what: Watch which third-party evaluators get named in any adopted framework and who funds them — a concentrated, lab-funded evaluator pool undermines the independence the framework claims to offer.
insights.quote: A pool of “independent” evaluators that is already remarkably small, funded by the same handful of organizations repeatedly relied upon by the same frontier labs.
insights.locator: The entry requirements set out in the proposal

insights.claim: Gomez proposes an internationally-coordinated, publicly-developed evidence-based risk framework — not led by any single nation, funded through public research bodies rather than the companies being measured, and binding rules based on what an AI system can do rather than who built it.
insights.speaker: Aidan Gomez
insights.so_what: A capability-based (not developer-based) rule structure is the alternative regulatory design to watch for as a less-captured model than the compute-threshold approach in Anthropic's roadmap.
insights.quote: write rules that bind based on what an AI system can do rather than on who built it, so a dangerous capability is treated the same whether it comes out of a trillion dollar lab or a university department
insights.locator: An evidence-based risk framework pillar

insights.claim: Gomez calls for mandatory transparency beyond today's model cards, extending to how companies across the AI development and deployment stack report serious incidents, with real accountability mechanisms attached when harm occurs.
insights.speaker: Aidan Gomez
insights.so_what: Mandatory incident-reporting requirements, if adopted, would create a new compliance and disclosure obligation across the AI industry worth tracking for regulatory-cost modeling.
insights.locator: Mandatory transparency pillar

insights.claim: Gomez's testing pillar calls for tiered, proportionate testing scoped only to capabilities the evidence-based framework has identified as genuinely dangerous — naming cyberattacks, synthetic fraud, voice cloning, manipulation at scale, physical or biochemical weapons, and critical-infrastructure risk — with certification open to every company, not restricted to a designated tier of large developers.
insights.speaker: Aidan Gomez
insights.so_what: Names the specific risk categories Cohere thinks should actually be tested, useful as a checklist for what future AI safety legislation might target.
insights.quote: Test what can harm people and societies, and let evidence decide what requires testing rather than whoever holds the pen.
insights.locator: Testing, scoped by the evidence pillar

insights.claim: Gomez lays out three conditions for real assurance mechanisms: testing criteria must be collectively developed and published; third-party reviewers must represent a range of opinions and never be paid by the party they review; and findings must reach the public in an unconflicted way.
insights.speaker: Aidan Gomez
insights.so_what: A concrete test for whether any future AI evaluator/auditor regime is genuinely independent versus captured — useful diligence criteria for assessing announced AI safety-audit arrangements.
insights.quote: any involved third parties must have a mandate to include an array of opinions and never be paid by the party they're reviewing
insights.locator: Real assurance mechanisms pillar

themes.theme: The July Incident and the Limits of Compute-Threshold Regulation

insights.claim: Gomez says the safety failures reported in July occurred inside the two best-resourced AI labs in the world, which already had the largest safety teams and most internal review, and in one case an outside evaluator arrangement was already being stood up through METR as recently as February.
insights.speaker: Aidan Gomez
insights.so_what: Strong evidence that the governance mechanisms Anthropic's proposal would formalize (large safety teams, outside evaluator arrangements) were already in place when a real failure occurred, undercutting the case that more of the same would prevent future incidents.
insights.quote: The failures we saw reported in July happened inside the two best-resourced labs in the world, with the largest safety teams, the most internal review
insights.locator: The failures we saw reported in July

insights.claim: Gomez argues neither a capability threshold nor a compute limit would have caught the July failures, because the actual cause was the quality of the instructions given, weak controls around the test environment, and how long the agents operated without observation.
insights.speaker: Aidan Gomez
insights.so_what: Suggests compute/capability-threshold regulation targets the wrong variable; operational controls like observability and instruction quality may matter more for near-term agentic-AI risk than model scale.
insights.quote: A capability threshold would not have caught it, because those systems were actively being trained and evaluated to assess their capability.
insights.locator: A capability threshold would not have caught it

insights.claim: Gomez dismisses a departing lab researcher's warning that superintelligent systems will probably wipe out humanity within a decade, and a senior colleague's claim of above-10% odds, as unquantified gut feelings rather than mathematical analysis, despite acknowledging both are likely well-intentioned.
insights.speaker: Aidan Gomez
insights.so_what: Investors evaluating AI-safety-driven regulatory asks should discount headline extinction-probability figures as rhetorical rather than empirically grounded.
insights.quote: They are gut feelings, vibes, expressed as decimals, amplified by executives with vested interests
insights.locator: Earlier this week, a researcher quit a large lab

insights.claim: Gomez argues that existential-superintelligence narratives conveniently distract from real, present-day AI harms, citing voice-cloning tools cheaper than a phone bill that can empty a pensioner's bank account in minutes.
insights.speaker: Aidan Gomez
insights.so_what: Flags voice-cloning fraud as an under-addressed, near-term consumer-protection risk that current frontier-only safety regimes largely ignore — relevant to fraud/compliance exposure in financial services.
insights.quote: voice cloning tools cheaper than a phone bill can empty a pensioner's account in minutes
insights.locator: voice cloning tools cheaper than a phone bill

insights.claim: Cohere positions its business around deploying AI inside regulated, high-stakes institutions (banks, telecom networks, defense ministries) on infrastructure those institutions control, arguing security comes from sovereignty, local deployment, and vendor diversity rather than dependence on a single foreign monopoly.
insights.speaker: Aidan Gomez
insights.so_what: This is Cohere's explicit commercial differentiation versus hyperscale foundation-model API providers — a sovereign/on-prem enterprise AI angle competing for government and regulated-industry contracts.
insights.quote: Security comes from sovereignty, local deployment, and technological diversity.
insights.locator: We built Cohere precisely because of this reality

insights.claim: Gomez argues a competitive market with many capable AI suppliers can absorb the failure of any single one, whereas a state-sanctioned cartel structure has no redundancy if it fails.
insights.speaker: Aidan Gomez
insights.so_what: Systemic-risk argument for supplier diversity in critical AI infrastructure — relevant to how governments and enterprises should structure AI vendor concentration risk.
insights.quote: A competitive market with many capable suppliers can absorb a failure at one of them. A state-sanctioned cartel has nowhere to hide one.
insights.locator: A competitive market with many capable suppliers

insights.claim: Gomez calls for AI rulemaking to include academics with no commercial stake, civil society groups who think the industry is moving too fast, smaller labs, open-source developers, and independent governments — explicitly including voices that would rule against Cohere itself.
insights.speaker: Aidan Gomez
insights.so_what: Signals Cohere's public policy positioning as pro-broad-stakeholder governance, a reputational and lobbying stance worth tracking alongside any actual policy engagement Cohere takes.
insights.quote: Academics with no commercial stake. Civil society groups who think everyone in this industry is moving too fast. Smaller labs and open-source developers.
insights.locator: A process worth having would include people
